claims.source: Our study was also motivated by human psychophysical studies that showed that body and head orientation interact in social perception (Hietanen, 2002; Moors et al., 2015; Vrancken et al., 2017), although it is unclear at which level – sensory or higher – the observed interactions occurred.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of previous research.

claims.claim: Behavioral studies in humans and monkeys provided evidence for greater body discrimination for upright compared to inverted bodies.
claims.source: Behavioral studies in humans (Griffin and Oswald, 2022) and monkeys (Matsuno and Fujita, 2018) provided evidence for greater body discrimination for upright compared to inverted bodies.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The body-inversion effect has been interpreted as providing evidence for the holistic encoding of bodies, similar to that proposed for faces.
claims.source: This body-inversion effect has been interpreted as providing evidence for the holistic encoding of bodies, similar to that proposed for faces.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about how previous findings have been interpreted in the literature.

claims.claim: Some studies suggested that the body-inversion effect is driven by the head.
claims.source: Some studies suggested that the body-inversion effect is driven by the head (for review, see Griffin and Oswald, 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review.

claims.claim: Other studies have observed a behavioral body-inversion effect for headless bodies.
claims.source: However, other studies have observed a behavioral body-inversion effect for headless bodies (for a meta-analysis, see Griffin and Oswald, 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a meta-analysis.

claims.claim: No neural correlates of the body-inversion effect for whole bodies have been described at the single-unit level prior to this study.
claims.source: So far, no neural correlates of the body-inversion effect for whole bodies have been described at the single-unit level.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature prior to the current study.

claims.claim: The study recorded responses of units at two posterior–anterior levels of the ventral STS, in and surrounding patches that were activated more by images of monkeys compared to objects in an fMRI study with the same subjects.
claims.source: We recorded the responses of units at two posterior–anterior levels of the ventral STS, in and surrounding patches that were activated more by images of monkeys compared to objects in an fMRI study with the same subjects (Zafirova et al., 2022; Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental approach and references a figure showing the recording locations.

claims.claim: Face–body interactions are more prominent in anterior IT.
claims.source: Because it has been proposed that face–body interactions are more prominent in anterior IT (Fisher and Freiwald, 2015; Hu et al., 2020; Zafirova et al., 2022), we expected stronger head–body orientation interactions in the anterior STS (aSTS).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The study expected stronger head–body orientation interactions in the anterior STS (aSTS).
claims.source: Because it has been proposed that face–body interactions are more prominent in anterior IT (Fisher and Freiwald, 2015; Hu et al., 2020; Zafirova et al., 2022), we expected stronger head–body orientation interactions in the anterior STS (aSTS).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors based on previous literature.

claims.claim: In experiment 1, 98 aSTS and 100 mSTS neurons were selected for further examination based on their responses to monkeys, faces, or bodies compared to object controls.
claims.source: We took neurons (Materials and methods) for further examination when their mean net response to the monkey, face, or body was at least twice the mean response to the corresponding object control condition. Thus, we obtained 98 aSTS and 100 mSTS neurons, split approximately equally across the two subjects.
claims.evidence: This describes the neuron selection criteria and the resulting sample sizes.

claims.claim: In both aSTS and mSTS regions, the averaged responses of the selected neurons were strongest for the monkey images, followed closely by the body and the face, and much weaker for the objects.
claims.source: In both regions, the averaged responses of the selected neurons were strongest for the monkey images, followed closely by the body and the face, and much weaker for the objects (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This describes the response pattern observed in the data, with reference to a figure.

claims.claim: Some neurons responded stronger to faces than bodies, or vice versa, and showed strong selectivity for different body or face images.
claims.source: Some neurons responded stronger to faces than bodies, or vice versa, and showed strong selectivity for different body or face images (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This describes variability in neuronal responses observed in the data.

claims.claim: For both subjects and regions, the median MSIs for P1 and P2 were smaller than 0.
claims.source: For both subjects and regions, the median MSIs for P1 and P2 were smaller than 0 (Figure 3A), which agrees with a single-unit study in anterior IT that employed images of real macaques (Zafirova et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This describes a finding from the data analysis, with reference to a figure and comparison to previous work.

claims.claim: Neurons were observed that responded to either the headless body or head but did not respond to the whole monkey that included the same body and head.
claims.source: Surprisingly, we observed neurons that responded to either the headless body or head but did not respond to the whole monkey that included the same body and head (MSI close to –1; Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This describes a specific observation from the data.

claims.claim: The weak responses to the monkey were not limited to cases in which the head–body configuration was anatomically impossible.
claims.source: The weak responses to the monkey were not limited to cases in which the head–body configuration was anatomically impossible, that is a straight angle between the head and the body.
claims.evidence: This describes a pattern observed in the data regarding anatomically possible vs. impossible configurations.

claims.claim: Cases in which MSI was between –0.9 and –1 included 53% and 41% of natural head–body configurations in aSTS and mSTS, respectively.
claims.source: In fact, cases in which MSI was between –0.9 and –1 included 53% and 41% of natural head–body configurations in aSTS and mSTS, respectively.
claims.evidence: This provides specific quantitative data about the proportion of natural configurations with very negative MSI values.

claims.claim: Only a minority of neurons demonstrated strong superadditive responses to the monkey (MSI between 0.9 and 1: 4.3% and 6.2% in aSTS and mSTS, respectively).
claims.source: In line with a previous study (Zafirova et al., 2024), only a minority of neurons demonstrated strong superadditive responses to the monkey (MSI between 0.9 and 1: 4.3% and 6.2% in aSTS and mSTS, respectively).
claims.evidence: This provides specific quantitative data about the proportion of neurons with superadditive responses, with comparison to previous work.

claims.claim: Heads and bodies interact at the level of the STS.
claims.source: These data show that heads and bodies interact at the level of the STS.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MSI analysis data.

claims.claim: The large majority of neurons showed a significant main effect (p < 0.05) of body orientation followed by a main effect of head orientation.
claims.source: The large majority of neurons showed a significant main effect (p < 0.05) of body orientation followed by a main effect of head orientation (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This describes the results of two-way ANOVA analyses on neuronal responses.

claims.claim: A large fraction of neurons showed a significant interaction between head and body orientation for both centerings (MC and HC) and poses (P1 and P2) in each region (aSTS and mSTS).
claims.source: Importantly, a large fraction of neurons showed a significant interaction between head and body orientation. This was true for both centerings (MC and HC) and poses (P1 and P2) in each region (aSTS and mSTS, Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This describes a key finding from the two-way ANOVA analyses.

claims.claim: The median correlations of responses to the 64 head–body configurations between MC and HC were 0.68 and 0.57 in aSTS and mSTS, respectively, indicating position tolerance of the orientation selectivity in both regions.
claims.source: The median correlations were 0.68 and 0.57 in aSTS and mSTS, respectively (Figure 3C), indicating position tolerance of the orientation selectivity in both regions.
claims.evidence: This describes quantitative results from correlation analyses assessing position tolerance.

claims.claim: aSTS showed significantly higher correlations than mSTS (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p = 0.008).
claims.source: In line with its higher hierarchical stage and thus expected higher location tolerance, aSTS showed significantly higher correlations than mSTS (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p = 0.008; tested after averaging the correlation coefficients of the poses per neuron; n = 75 aSTS and n = 77 mSTS neurons).
claims.evidence: This describes a statistical comparison between the two regions.

claims.claim: The higher correlations for aSTS were not a result of differences in response reliability between the two regions.
claims.source: The higher correlations for aSTS were not a result of differences in response reliability between the two regions: the median Spearman–Brown corrected split-half Pearson correlation (Materials and methods) was 0.82 and 0.81 for the MC and HC aSTS neurons (n = 131 cases) and 0.85 and 0.89 for the MC and HC mSTS neurons (n = 126 cases).
claims.evidence: This describes reliability analyses that rule out an alternative explanation for the regional difference.

claims.claim: The relatively higher reliability for mSTS shows that the lower correlation of the head–body orientation selectivity between the two centerings for mSTS neurons is not due to lower reliability.
claims.source: The relatively higher reliability for mSTS shows that the lower correlation of the head–body orientation selectivity between the two centerings for mSTS neurons is not due to lower reliability.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the reliability data.

claims.claim: Correcting the correlations for reliability showed a lower median corrected correlation for mSTS (median: 0.72) compared to aSTS (0.90).
claims.source: Furthermore, correcting the correlations for reliability showed a lower median corrected correlation for mSTS (median: 0.72) compared to aSTS (0.90).
claims.evidence: This describes the results of reliability-corrected correlation analyses.

claims.claim: In aSTS, 24% of the neurons responding for both centerings of a pose (n = 135) showed a significant interaction in both centerings, and this proportion was similar for mSTS (26%; n = 127).
claims.source: In aSTS, 24% of the neurons responding for both centerings of a pose (n = 135) showed a significant interaction in both centerings, and this proportion was similar for mSTS (26%; n = 127; Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This provides quantitative data on the proportion of neurons showing position-tolerant interactions.

claims.claim: For neuron and pose combinations with significant head–body interactions in both centerings, the correlations between responses to the 64 head–body orientation conditions were similar to those observed in the whole population.
claims.source: Notably, for neuron and pose combinations with significant head–body interactions in both centerings, the correlations between responses to the 64 head–body orientation conditions were similar to those observed in the whole population (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This describes a comparison of correlation values for a subset of neurons.

claims.claim: The median correlation between the residuals of the two centerings was 0.23 (quartiles: 0.08–0.36; n = 33) for mSTS.
claims.source: The median correlation between the residuals of the two centerings was 0.23 (quartiles: 0.08–0.36; n = 33) for mSTS, whereas it was 0.41 (0.21–0.55; n = 33; median larger than 0: p = 9.35e−07) for aSTS, which was significantly greater than for mSTS (Wilcoxon rank-sum test; p = 0.008).
claims.evidence: This describes quantitative results from residual correlation analyses.

claims.claim: The median correlation between the residuals of the two centerings was 0.41 (0.21–0.55; n = 33; median larger than 0: p = 9.35e−07) for aSTS, which was significantly greater than for mSTS (Wilcoxon rank-sum test; p = 0.008).
claims.source: The median correlation between the residuals of the two centerings was 0.23 (quartiles: 0.08–0.36; n = 33) for mSTS, whereas it was 0.41 (0.21–0.55; n = 33; median larger than 0: p = 9.35e−07) for aSTS, which was significantly greater than for mSTS (Wilcoxon rank-sum test; p = 0.008).
claims.evidence: This describes quantitative results from residual correlation analyses with statistical testing.

claims.claim: The data demonstrate a position tolerance of the interaction of head and body orientation in aSTS, but less so in mSTS.
claims.source: These data demonstrate a position tolerance of the interaction of head and body orientation in aSTS, but less so in mSTS.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the residual correlation analyses.

claims.claim: Some neurons were tuned to a particular combination of a head and body orientation irrespective of centering.
claims.source: Interestingly, some neurons (e.g. Figure 3D) were tuned to a particular combination of a head and body orientation irrespective of centering (e.g. the third aSTS example neuron of Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This describes an observation from example neurons shown in a figure.

claims.claim: The tuning for head–body orientation generalized across the two poses for the population of mSTS and aSTS neurons that responded significantly to each pose.
claims.source: The tuning for head–body orientation generalized across the two poses for the population of mSTS and aSTS neurons that responded significantly to each pose (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This describes a finding from correlation analyses across poses, shown in a supplementary figure.

claims.claim: For the zero and straight reference angles, the classification accuracy increased with the absolute difference between the angles, reaching a maximum of about 0.7 classification accuracy for zero versus straight angles.
claims.source: For the zero and straight reference angles, the classification accuracy increased with the absolute difference between the angles, reaching a maximum of about 0.7 classification accuracy for zero versus straight angles.
claims.evidence: This describes a pattern observed in the decoding analyses.

claims.claim: Classification accuracies were smaller for mSTS compared to aSTS.
claims.source: Classification accuracies were smaller for mSTS compared to aSTS.
claims.evidence: This describes a comparison of decoding performance between regions.

claims.claim: For the rightward (90°) and leftward (–90°) right angles as references, classification scores were low, which contrasts with the higher scores for the same 180° orientation difference when the angles were zero and straight.
claims.source: Surprisingly, for the rightward (90°) and leftward (–90°) right angles as references, classification scores were low (Figure 4B), which contrasts with the higher scores for the same 180° orientation difference when the angles were zero and straight (this difference was significant for both centerings and poses in aSTS; all p-values <0.01).
claims.evidence: This describes a surprising pattern in the decoding results with statistical testing.

claims.claim: Classification scores tended to be higher for 90° differences in angles (e.g. right vs. straight) than for the 180° difference (rightward vs. leftward right angles) for the rightward or leftward right reference angles.
claims.source: Classification scores tended to be higher for 90° differences in angles (e.g. right vs. straight) than for the 180° difference (rightward vs. leftward right angles) for the rightward or leftward right reference angles.
claims.evidence: This describes a pattern observed in the decoding analyses.

claims.claim: The decoding accuracies showed the same pattern, although were higher, when training and testing were performed with the same centering, requiring no generalization across locations.
claims.source: The decoding accuracies showed the same pattern, although were higher, when training and testing were performed with the same centering, requiring no generalization across locations (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This describes results from additional decoding analyses shown in a supplementary figure.

claims.claim: A neuron-dropping analysis applied to the decoding of zero versus straight angles for the aSTS sample suggested that less than half of the neurons contributed positively to the decoding.
claims.source: A neuron-dropping analysis applied to the decoding of zero versus straight angles for the aSTS sample (MC training and HC testing) suggested that less than half of the neurons contributed positively to the decoding (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This describes results from a neuron-dropping analysis shown in a supplementary figure.

claims.claim: Most but not all of the 10 'best' neurons showed a significant interaction between head and body orientation.
claims.source: Most but not all of the 10 'best' neurons, that is those that contributed most to the decoding, showed a significant interaction between head and body orientation.
claims.evidence: This describes a finding from the neuron-dropping analysis regarding the properties of the most informative neurons.

claims.claim: More of the 10 'best' neurons (at least 50% (95% confidence interval: 19–81%)) showed individually a significant effect of head–body orientation angle on their responses than expected for a random sample of the population of neurons (maximal expected percentage 16%).
claims.source: Furthermore, more of the 10 'best' neurons (at least 50% (95% confidence interval: 19–81%)) showed individually a significant effect of head–body orientation angle on their responses (one-way ANOVA; p < 0.05) than expected for a random sample of the population of neurons (maximal expected percentage 16%; see Figure 4—figure supplement 2 for more details).
claims.evidence: This describes a statistical comparison of the properties of the best neurons versus the population.

claims.claim: The tuning profiles of the 'best' neurons were diverse, suggesting population coding of head–body orientation angle.
claims.source: Nonetheless, the tuning profiles were diverse (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting population coding of head–body orientation angle.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the diversity of tuning profiles observed in the data.

claims.claim: For P1, the performance accuracies for the aSTS sample were well above chance for the zero versus straight angle decoding when training and testing on different orientations.
claims.source: For P1, the performance accuracies for the aSTS sample were well above chance for the zero versus straight angle decoding, and, as before, were lower for the leftward versus rightward right angle decoding (Figure 5B; for brevity, we will refer to these angles as left and right angles, respectively, below).
claims.evidence: This describes results from a more stringent decoding analysis with generalization across orientations.

claims.claim: For P2, the performance accuracies for zero versus straight angles were barely above chance and were at a similar level as those for the right versus left angle decoding for two of the four centering and orientation training–test combinations.
claims.source: However, for the other two combinations, the performance accuracies for the zero versus straight angles were barely above chance and were at a similar level as those for the right versus left angle decoding (Figure 5B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This describes results from the decoding analysis for P2 showing different patterns for different training-test combinations.

claims.claim: The interaction between generalization across orientation and centering for P2 is likely related to the larger variations in the eccentricity of the head when changing the orientation and centering of the standing avatar.
claims.source: This interaction between generalization across orientation and centering for P2 is likely related to the larger variations in the eccentricity of the head when changing the orientation and centering of the standing avatar (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the cause of the observed pattern, with reference to a supplementary figure.

claims.claim: When generalization across orientation but not across centering was required, accuracies for P1 and P2 were similar for all decodings.
claims.source: Nonetheless, when generalization across orientation but not across centering was required, accuracies for P1 and P2 were similar for all decodings (for the zero vs. straight angle: classification accuracies for P1 ranging from 0.64 to 0.72 and for P2 ranging from 0.66 to 0.72; for the right vs. left angle decoding: P1 0.49–0.54 and P2 0.48–0.56).
claims.evidence: This describes results from decoding analyses without generalization across centering.

claims.claim: The marked difference in accuracy between the zero versus straight angle decoding and the right versus left angle decoding in aSTS was not trivially due to differences in mean response strength since there was no consistent effect of head–body orientation angle on mean response strength across poses.
claims.source: The marked difference in accuracy between the zero versus straight angle decoding and the right versus left angle decoding in aSTS was not trivially due to differences in mean response strength since there was no consistent effect of head–body orientation angle on mean response strength across poses (Friedman ANOVA; all p-values for both poses and centerings >0.1).
claims.evidence: This describes a control analysis ruling out an alternative explanation for the decoding results.

claims.claim: The confusion between left and right angle configurations suggests that this neuronal population is relatively insensitive to the sign of the angle.
claims.source: The left and right angles have the same absolute angle between head and body (90°), only the sign of the angle differs with respect to the anatomical midline (90° vs. –90°). The confusion between these configurations suggests that this neuronal population is relatively insensitive to the sign of the angle.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the decoding results.

claims.claim: Close-to-chance decoding was observed for 45° versus –45° angles and 135° versus –135° angles.
claims.source: We observed a close-to-chance decoding of 45° versus –45° angles and 135° versus –135° angles, unlike the better classification accuracy for the same 90° differences between angles of 0° and 90° or 180° and –90°, the latter but not the former differing in the absolute angle between head and body.
claims.evidence: This describes additional decoding results supporting the insensitivity to sign.

claims.claim: Configurations that differ in absolute angle (45° versus –135° and 135° versus –45°) produced good decoding performance, better than the left versus right angles, which differed only in sign.
claims.source: Other configurations that differ in absolute angle also produced good decoding performance: 45° versus –135° and 135° versus –45°, better than the left versus right angles, which differed only in sign (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This describes additional decoding results supporting the importance of absolute angle differences.

claims.claim: Neurons in anterior IT are less sensitive to differences between mirror-symmetric images.
claims.source: Neurons in anterior IT are less sensitive to differences between mirror-symmetric images (Freiwald and Tsao, 2010; Rollenhagen and Olson, 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The distance matrices showed evidence for mirror-symmetric responses for the lateral head and body orientations for P2 and face orientations of P1.
claims.source: The distance matrices showed evidence for mirror-symmetric responses for the lateral head and body orientations for P2 and face orientations of P1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This describes results from distance matrix analyses shown in a supplementary figure.

claims.claim: Mirror symmetry was less the case for the body of P1, which fits the poorer image symmetry of the body in the case of the P1 lateral views.
claims.source: Mirror symmetry was less the case for the body of P1, which fits the poorer image symmetry of the body in the case of the P1 lateral views.
claims.evidence: This is an inference relating the neural data to properties of the stimuli.

claims.claim: The lower sensitivity for mirror-symmetric heads or bodies may have contributed to the lower decoding of head–body angles that differed only in their sign.
claims.source: Thus, the lower sensitivity for mirror-symmetric heads or bodies may have contributed to the lower decoding of head–body angles that differed only in their sign.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about a potential mechanism underlying the observed decoding pattern.

claims.claim: The difference in decoding accuracy between the zero versus straight angle and the left versus right angle cannot be fully attributed to the mirror symmetry of the avatar images.
claims.source: However, the difference in decoding accuracy between the zero versus straight angle and the left versus right angle, especially when training on the 'x' orientations and testing on '+' orientations (Figure 5), cannot be fully attributed to the mirror symmetry of the avatar images.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the decoding analyses that rules out mirror symmetry as the sole explanation.

claims.claim: Spike sorting yielded 497 aSTS (M1 = 280; M2 = 217) and 1856 mSTS (M1 = 804; M2 = 1052) units that responded selectively to the 16 monkey conditions in experiment 2.
claims.source: Spike sorting yielded 497 aSTS (M1 = 280; M2 = 217) and 1856 mSTS (M1 = 804; M2 = 1052) units that responded selectively to the 16 monkey conditions (Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This describes the sample sizes obtained in experiment 2.

claims.claim: A highly similar pattern of decoding was found in experiment 2 compared to that obtained with the smaller sample of single units of experiment 1.
claims.source: We found a highly similar pattern (n = 430 units; equated across the two regions and subjects; randomly sampled per subject per resampling; Figure 6B) compared to that obtained with the smaller sample of single units of experiment 1 (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This describes a replication of the main decoding findings in a larger sample.

claims.claim: For aSTS in experiment 2, the classification accuracy for the zero versus straight angles was about 0.9.
claims.source: For aSTS, the classification accuracy for the zero versus straight angles was about 0.9 (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This describes a specific decoding result from experiment 2.

claims.claim: In experiment 2, classification accuracy for the right versus left angles was much lower than that obtained for zero versus right angle, or straight versus left angle, differing in absolute angle (p < 0.01).
claims.source: Again, classification accuracy for the right versus left angles, differing only in their sign, was much lower than that obtained for zero versus right angle, or straight versus left angle, differing in absolute angle (Figure 6B; p < 0.01).
claims.evidence: This describes a replication of the key decoding pattern in experiment 2 with statistical testing.

claims.claim: The classification accuracy for mSTS units in experiment 2 was again lower than for aSTS, although no generalization across centering conditions was required for this decoding.
claims.source: The classification accuracy for mSTS units was again lower than for aSTS (Figure 6B), although no generalization across centering conditions was required for this decoding.
claims.evidence: This describes a regional difference in decoding performance in experiment 2.

claims.claim: In mSTS in experiment 2, there was no difference in decoding accuracy for the zero versus straight angle and right versus left angle.
claims.source: Importantly, in mSTS there was no difference in decoding accuracy for the zero versus straight angle and right versus left angle.
claims.evidence: This describes a key difference between aSTS and mSTS in the decoding pattern.

claims.claim: The reliability of the responses of the units was similar for aSTS (median Spearman–Brown corrected split-half Pearson correlation; M1: 0.70; M2: 0.69) and mSTS (median corrected r: M1: 0.72; M2: 0.71) in experiment 2.
claims.source: The reliability of the responses of the units was similar for aSTS (median Spearman–Brown corrected split-half Pearson correlation; M1: 0.70; M2: 0.69) and mSTS (median corrected r: M1: 0.72; M2: 0.71) and therefore cannot explain the difference in classification accuracy between the two regions.
claims.evidence: This describes reliability analyses that rule out an alternative explanation for regional differences.

claims.claim: For aSTS in experiment 2, the classification accuracies for the head–body sums were markedly lower than those obtained for the monkey images.
claims.source: For aSTS, the classification accuracies for the sums were markedly lower than those obtained for the monkey images (Figure 6B), and no difference in classification accuracy between the zero versus straight angles and left versus right angles was present for the sums (all p's > 0.4).
claims.evidence: This describes results from decoding analyses using summed responses to isolated heads and bodies.

claims.claim: For aSTS in experiment 2, no difference in classification accuracy between the zero versus straight angles and left versus right angles was present for the head–body sums (all p's > 0.4).
claims.source: For aSTS, the classification accuracies for the sums were markedly lower than those obtained for the monkey images (Figure 6B), and no difference in classification accuracy between the zero versus straight angles and left versus right angles was present for the sums (all p's > 0.4).
claims.evidence: This describes a key finding from the sum decoding analysis.

claims.claim: The lower classification accuracy for the head–body sums in aSTS is not due to a lower reliability of the summed responses compared to the whole-body responses.
claims.source: The lower classification accuracy for the head–body sums is not due to a lower reliability of the summed responses compared to the whole-body responses (Spearman–Brown corrected split-half Pearson correlations; median whole-body r: M1: 0.7; M2: 0.69; sums r: M1: 0.76; M2: 0.66).
claims.evidence: This describes reliability analyses that rule out an alternative explanation.

claims.claim: The difference in classification accuracy between the zero versus straight angles and left versus right angles requires the simultaneous presence of the head and body.
claims.source: These data suggest that the difference in classification accuracy between the zero versus straight angles and left versus right angles requires the simultaneous presence of the head and body.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of decoding for whole monkeys versus summed head and body responses.

claims.claim: For mSTS in experiment 2, the classification accuracies for the head–body sums were similar to those obtained for the monkey images.
claims.source: For mSTS, the classification accuracies for the head–body sums were similar to those obtained for the monkey images (Figure 6B), suggesting no genuine encoding of the head–body angle in this region.
claims.evidence: This describes results from the sum decoding analysis for mSTS.

claims.claim: The similar classification accuracies for head–body sums and monkey images in mSTS suggest no genuine encoding of the head–body angle in this region.
claims.source: For mSTS, the classification accuracies for the head–body sums were similar to those obtained for the monkey images (Figure 6B), suggesting no genuine encoding of the head–body angle in this region.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the mSTS sum decoding results.

claims.claim: Head- and body-selective aSTS units showed, as a population, a similar decoding bias for zero versus straight angles and both confused the left and right angles.
claims.source: Head- and body-selective aSTS units showed, as a population, a similar decoding bias for zero versus straight angles and both confused the left and right angles (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This describes results from analyses subdividing units by head/body selectivity.

claims.claim: A higher mean response was observed for the upright compared to the inverted preferred orientation of the whole monkey for each pose, in each region of each subject in experiment 3.
claims.source: We observed for each pose, in each region of each subject, a higher mean response for the upright compared to the inverted preferred orientation of the whole monkey (Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on data pooled across monkeys: p's in Figure 7C; population PSTHs (Peri-Stimulus Time Histograms) in Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This describes a key finding from experiment 3 regarding the body-inversion effect on response strength.

claims.claim: Upright heads showed across subjects consistently and significantly greater responses than to inverted heads only for P2 in mSTS but not for the other pose or region.
claims.source: Selecting units that responded either to the upright or inverted heads showed less consistent inversion effects for the head than observed for the monkey: upright heads showed across subjects consistently and significantly greater responses than to inverted heads only for P2 in mSTS but not for the other pose or region (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This describes results from analyses of responses to isolated heads in experiment 3.

claims.claim: The inversion effect for headless bodies was less consistent than for the whole monkey in experiment 3.
claims.source: The same held for the headless body for those units that responded to either the upright or inverted bodies (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This describes results from analyses of responses to isolated bodies in experiment 3.

claims.claim: The inversion effect was consistently present for the head–body configurations, and less so for the face and body only.
claims.source: Thus, the inversion effect was consistently present for the head–body configurations, and less so for the face and body only.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the inversion effect analyses in experiment 3.

claims.claim: The mean decoding accuracy was significantly higher (all p-values <0.01) for upright compared to inverted monkeys for both poses in aSTS (P1: upright versus inverted: 0.89 vs. 0.82; P2: 0.89 vs. 0.71, with standard deviations SD = 0.02) and mSTS (P1: 0.89 vs. 0.79; P2: 0.93 vs. 0.75; SDs ranging between 0.01 and 0.02).

results.result: STS neurons show significant interactions between head and body orientation, with position-tolerant interactions more prominent in aSTS than mSTS. A large fraction of neurons in both regions showed significant head-body orientation interactions, with aSTS demonstrating greater position tolerance of these interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36 demonstrate significant main effects and interactions in two-way ANOVAs across both regions and conditions. Claims C44-C46 provide quantitative evidence (median correlations, residual analyses with p-values) showing position tolerance is significantly greater in aSTS (r=0.41, p=9.35e-07) than mSTS (r=0.23). The statistical tests are appropriate and the conclusions (C34, C7) follow logically from the data.

results.result: aSTS neurons enable superior decoding of head-body configuration angles compared to mSTS, with highest accuracy for zero versus straight angles (0.7-0.9) and lowest for angles differing only in sign (±90°). This pattern was replicated across experiments 1 and 2.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 describe the decoding pattern in experiment 1 with statistical significance (p<0.01). Claims C72-C74 replicate these findings in experiment 2 with a larger sample (n=430 units) showing classification accuracy ~0.9 for zero vs straight angles. The regional difference (C3, C50, C112) is consistently demonstrated across experiments with appropriate controls for reliability (C77).

results.result: In aSTS, decoding of head-body angle from summed responses to isolated heads and bodies was markedly lower than from whole-body images and eliminated the differential decoding pattern, suggesting genuine integration requires simultaneous presence of head and body. In mSTS, summed responses produced similar decoding to whole-body images.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C79 show that in aSTS, summed responses produced lower accuracy and no difference between angle pairs (p>0.4), contrasting with whole-body responses. Reliability analyses (C80) rule out alternative explanations. Claims C82-C83 show mSTS summed and whole-body responses were similar, supporting the inference that mSTS lacks genuine head-body angle encoding. The logic is sound and controls are appropriate.

results.result: Body inversion impairs neural responses and head-body angle decoding in STS. Upright bodies showed consistently higher responses than inverted bodies for whole-body configurations, and decoding accuracy dropped significantly for inverted bodies (p<0.01), with larger drops for zero versus straight angles than for left versus right angles.
results.evaluation: Claim C85 reports consistent inversion effects across poses and regions with statistical testing (Wilcoxon tests, p-values in Figure 7C). Claims C91-C92 show significant drops in decoding accuracy (p<0.01) with differential effects by angle type. Claim C88 notes the effect was more consistent for whole bodies than isolated parts. The unbiased unit selection (both upright and inverted) strengthens the finding (C122). This is the first demonstration at single-unit level (C120).

results.result: aSTS neurons show relative insensitivity to the sign of head-body angles, confusing configurations differing only in sign (e.g., ±90°). This pattern was robust across three experiments and may be partially explained by mirror symmetry sensitivity, though mirror symmetry alone cannot fully account for the effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C65 provide specific decoding results showing close-to-chance performance for angles differing only in sign but good performance for angles differing in absolute value. Claim C102 emphasizes robustness across three experiments. Claims C67, C104 provide evidence for mirror-symmetric responses in distance matrices. However, claim C70 appropriately notes mirror symmetry cannot fully explain the pattern. The inference (C63, C105) is reasonable but acknowledged as partial.

results.result: Responses to whole monkeys were generally subadditive (median MSI < 0), with some neurons showing strong suppression (MSI near -1) even for anatomically possible configurations. Only a minority showed superadditive responses (4.3-6.2%).
results.evaluation: Claim C29 reports median MSI < 0 across subjects, regions, and poses, with citation to consistent prior work. Claims C30-C32 provide specific quantitative data about the distribution of MSI values, including the surprising finding that 53% and 41% of very negative MSI cases (-0.9 to -1) included natural configurations. Claim C33 quantifies the minority showing superaddition. The data are clearly presented with appropriate statistics.

results.result: aSTS shows significantly higher position tolerance of head-body orientation selectivity than mSTS (median correlations 0.68 vs 0.57, p=0.008), which is not explained by differences in response reliability between regions.
results.evaluation: Claim C37 provides quantitative correlation values with statistical testing (p=0.008). Claims C39-C40 present reliability analyses showing mSTS actually had slightly higher reliability, ruling out this alternative explanation. Claim C41 shows reliability-corrected correlations maintain the regional difference (0.90 vs 0.72). The logic is sound and appropriate controls are included.

results.result: When requiring generalization across both orientation and centering, decoding accuracy varied by pose and training-test combination, with P2 showing interactions likely related to head eccentricity variations. Without centering generalization, P1 and P2 showed similar accuracies.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C59 describe the differential performance across conditions with specific accuracy values. Claim C60 provides a plausible mechanistic explanation with reference to supplementary data. Claim C61 shows that removing centering generalization eliminates the interaction, supporting the interpretation. The pattern is complex but the data and interpretation are internally consistent.

results.result: Neuron-dropping analysis suggests less than half of aSTS neurons contributed positively to head-body angle decoding. The 'best' neurons showed diverse tuning profiles and were enriched for significant head-body angle effects (≥50%) compared to the population (≤16%).
results.evaluation: Claim C54 describes the neuron-dropping result with reference to supplementary figure. Claims C55-C56 provide quantitative characterization of the best neurons with confidence intervals and statistical comparisons to expected values. Claim C57 draws the appropriate inference about population coding from the diversity of tuning. The analysis is appropriate for understanding which neurons contribute to decoding.

results.result: Head- and body-selective aSTS units showed similar decoding patterns for head-body angles, both showing bias for zero versus straight angles and confusion of left versus right angles.
results.evaluation: Claim C84 is supported by supplementary figure analyses that subdivided units by selectivity. This demonstrates the decoding pattern is not driven by a specific subpopulation but is a general property of aSTS units responsive to heads or bodies.

results.result: Decoding of whole-body orientation was significantly more accurate for upright than inverted monkeys in both aSTS and mSTS for both poses (all p<0.01), with accuracy differences ranging from 0.07 to 0.18.
results.evaluation: Claim C89 provides specific quantitative accuracy values with standard deviations and statistical significance (p<0.01) for all conditions. The effect is consistent across regions and poses, supporting a robust body-inversion effect on orientation discrimination.

results.result: Inversion effects for isolated heads and bodies were less consistent than for whole-body configurations, with significant effects for heads only in P2 mSTS.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87 describe analyses of isolated body parts with reference to supplementary figures. The finding that inversion effects are more consistent for whole bodies than parts supports the interpretation that the effect depends on the complete configuration.

results.result: The stronger inversion effect for zero versus straight angle decoding and the generalization across orientations in experiment 1 suggest the head-body angle signal depends on global configuration rather than local features.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C95 draw inferences from the pattern of inversion effects and generalization results. The logic is sound: if local features drove decoding, orientation generalization would not be expected, and inversion (which preserves local features) would not impair decoding. The inference is reasonable though not definitively proven.

results.result: In experiment 1, 98 aSTS and 100 mSTS neurons were selected based on responses at least twice as strong to monkeys, faces, or bodies compared to object controls. Averaged responses were strongest for monkeys, followed by bodies and faces, with individual neurons showing varied selectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C28 describe the neuron selection criteria and response patterns with reference to Figure 1B. The selection criterion (2x response to preferred category vs control) is clearly stated and the resulting sample sizes are reported. The response patterns are descriptive and supported by the figure.

results.result: About 24-26% of neurons showed significant head-body interactions in both centerings, and for these neurons, correlations between responses to the 64 configurations were similar to the whole population.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C43 provide specific percentages and describe the correlation pattern for the subset with position-tolerant interactions. This characterizes the proportion of neurons with robust, position-invariant interactions.

results.result: Some individual neurons showed tuning to specific head-body orientation combinations irrespective of centering, and tuning generalized across the two poses for responsive neurons.
results.evaluation: Claim C47 describes example neurons with reference to Figure 3D. Claim C48 reports population-level generalization across poses with reference to supplementary figure. These provide evidence for both single-neuron and population-level generalization.

results.result: The difference in decoding accuracy between zero versus straight angles and right versus left angles was not due to differences in mean response strength, as there was no consistent effect of head-body angle on mean response (Friedman ANOVA, all p>0.1).
results.evaluation: Claim C62 describes a control analysis with appropriate statistical testing (Friedman ANOVA) that rules out a simple alternative explanation based on response magnitude. This strengthens the interpretation that the decoding pattern reflects tuning differences rather than overall response strength.

results.result: Distance matrix analyses showed evidence for mirror-symmetric responses for lateral head and body orientations in P2 and face orientations in P1, with less mirror symmetry for P1 body, consistent with poorer image symmetry.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68 describe distance matrix results with reference to supplementary figure. The observation that neural mirror symmetry matches stimulus symmetry (C68) provides internal consistency. This supports the potential role of mirror symmetry in the decoding pattern.

results.result: Experiment 2 yielded 497 aSTS and 1856 mSTS units that responded selectively to the 16 monkey conditions.
results.evaluation: Claim C71 reports sample sizes for experiment 2 with breakdown by subject. This is straightforward descriptive data about the dataset.

results.result: In experiment 2, mSTS showed lower classification accuracy than aSTS and no difference between zero versus straight and right versus left angle decoding, despite similar response reliability between regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76 describe the regional differences in decoding patterns. Claim C77 provides reliability data ruling out this alternative explanation. This replicates and extends the experiment 1 findings regarding regional differences.

results.result: Lower classification accuracy for head-body sums in aSTS was not due to lower reliability of summed responses (median reliability: whole-body 0.69-0.70, sums 0.66-0.76).
results.evaluation: Claim C80 provides reliability data that rules out an alternative explanation for the lower sum decoding accuracy. The reliability of summed responses was actually similar or higher than whole-body responses.

results.result: The same population of neurons could decode the angle between head and body irrespective of the configuration's orientation.
results.evaluation: Claim C100 describes orientation-invariant decoding with reference to Figure 4A. This demonstrates that the neural population encodes head-body angle in a way that generalizes across viewpoints, which is computationally important for social perception.

results.result: The highest decoding occurred for zero versus straight angles (natural vs anatomically impossible), and all well-decodable angle pairs consisted of possible versus impossible angles. However, dissociating anatomical possibility from absolute angle difference and mirror symmetry is not trivial as these factors covary.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C107 describe the pattern of decodable angles and their relationship to anatomical possibility. Claim C108 offers this as a potential explanation. Claim C109 appropriately acknowledges the limitation that these factors cannot be dissociated with the current design. The reasoning is sound and limitations are acknowledged.

results.result: Decoding of whole-monkey orientation was present in both regions, consistent with previous studies, and decoding of head and body orientation was better in mSTS than aSTS, also consistent with prior work.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C111 report findings consistent with previous literature (with citations) and reference supplementary figure. These replicate known findings and provide context for the novel head-body angle decoding results.

results.result: No significant effect of head-body orientation angle on mean response strength was observed, indicating anatomically possible and impossible configurations elicited similar responses. However, as a population, neurons could distinguish these configurations well based on absolute angle differences.
results.evaluation: Claim C114 reports the absence of a mean response effect. Claims C117-C118 draw appropriate inferences: similar mean responses but different population-level discriminability. This demonstrates that information is in the pattern of responses across the population, not in overall response magnitude.

results.result: A previous study showing lower responses to misaligned head-body configurations targeted a partially overlapping patch and examined head-body relative position rather than orientation interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C116 compare the current study to previous work, noting differences in recording location and experimental manipulation. This appropriately contextualizes why results might differ from prior findings.

results.result: The regional difference in head-body configuration decoding agrees with previous work suggesting head-body integration is more prominent in anterior than posterior temporal cortex.
results.evaluation: Claim C113 relates the current findings to previous literature with appropriate citations. This places the results in the context of the broader understanding of temporal cortex organization.

results.result: Based on the electrophysiological data, discrimination of head-body orientation angle would be predicted to be more accurate for zero versus straight angles than right versus left angles at the behavioral level, but this requires psychophysical testing.
results.evaluation: Claim C119 makes a prediction based on the neural data but explicitly acknowledges it requires future behavioral testing. This is a reasonable prediction but cannot be evaluated as supported without the behavioral data.

results.result: Previous studies reported higher responses to upright versus inverted bodies in STS, but those neurons were searched with upright bodies. The current study avoided this search bias by selecting units using both upright and inverted images.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C122 compare the current methodology to previous studies, noting an important methodological improvement. The unbiased selection strengthens the interpretation of the inversion effect.

results.result: The current data suggest a more consistent inversion effect for head-body configurations compared to headless bodies and heads in STS.
results.evaluation: Claim C125 summarizes the pattern of inversion effects across stimulus types based on the data from experiment 3. This is a reasonable inference from claims C85-C88.

results.result: Monkeys were not exposed to anatomically impossible head-body orientations, yet responses to these were similar to anatomically possible configurations. The apparent discrepancy with the inversion effect may result from both head and body being in infrequent orientations for inversion, versus only one part for impossible configurations.
results.evaluation: Claim C127 notes an observation about the monkeys' experience and neural responses. Claim C128 offers a speculative explanation for why inversion has stronger effects than anatomical impossibility. This is labeled as speculation in the evidence type and remains unproven.

results.result: The study recorded from fMRI-defined monkey patches in two male rhesus monkeys with appropriate ethical approval.
results.evaluation: Claims C23, C129-C130 describe the subjects, recording locations, and ethical approval. These are straightforward methodological details that are clearly documented.

results.result: STS neurons show selectivity for specific combinations of head-body orientations, with significant interactions between head and body orientation demonstrated through two-way ANOVA analyses. A large fraction of neurons in both aSTS and mSTS showed significant interactions between head and body orientation across different centerings and poses, indicating that heads and bodies interact at the level of the STS.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm this core finding. Reviewer 1 states the study shows 'different neurons showed preferences for body orientation, or head orientation or for the interaction between the two.' Reviewer 2 notes 'STS neurons integrate head and body information in a nonlinear way, showing selectivity for specific combinations of head-body orientations.' Reviewer 3 similarly confirms 'STS neurons integrate head and body information in a nonlinear way.' No concerns are raised about this fundamental result.

results.result: Anterior STS (aSTS) neurons enabled more reliable decoding of head-body configuration angles compared to middle STS (mSTS) neurons, with higher position tolerance. The median correlations between MC and HC were 0.68 for aSTS and 0.57 for mSTS (p=0.008), and residual correlations were significantly higher in aSTS (0.41) than mSTS (0.23, p=0.008), demonstrating position-tolerant head-body orientation interactions in aSTS but less so in mSTS.
results.evaluation: Reviewers consistently affirm this regional difference. Reviewer 1 notes the study shows 'the neuronal population can decode head-body angle presented across orientations, in the anterior aSTS patch (but not middle mSTS patch)' and that 'mSTS neurons show less invariance for head-body angle.' Reviewer 2 states 'Head-body configuration angles can be reliably decoded, particularly for neurons in the anterior STS, suggesting a transformation of face/body orientation signals from the middle to the anterior STS.' No methodological concerns are raised about these analyses.

results.result: Decoding accuracy in aSTS was highest for aligned (0°) versus straight (180°) head-body orientations and lowest for configurations differing only in sign (±90°). This pattern was robust across three experiments, with classification accuracy reaching ~0.7-0.9 for zero versus straight angles but near chance for left versus right angles. The confusion between mirror-symmetric configurations suggests the neuronal population is relatively insensitive to the sign of the angle.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge this key finding. Reviewer 1 states the study shows 'the neuronal population can decode head-body angle presented across orientations, in the anterior aSTS patch (but not middle mSTS patch), except for mirror orientation.' Reviewer 2 notes 'these neurons distinguish aligned and opposite head-body configurations effectively, whereas mirror-symmetric configurations are more difficult to differentiate.' The robustness across experiments is implicitly accepted through the lack of critique.

results.result: Inverted bodies showed diminished decoding of head-body orientation angle compared to upright bodies, with a stronger inversion effect for zero versus straight angles than for left versus right angles. The inversion effect was consistently present for head-body configurations and less so for faces and bodies alone. This represents the first demonstration of an inversion effect for bodies with heads in the ventral bank of the STS at the single-unit level, without search bias confounds.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm this novel finding. Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'an upside-down inversion diminishes the encoding of head-body angles' as one of the three main findings. Reviewer 1 notes the study 'raises questions for future investigations comparing humans and monkeys expertise with upright and inverted configurations,' implicitly accepting the inversion effect results. No concerns are raised about the methodology or interpretation of the inversion experiments.

results.result: In aSTS, classification accuracies for summed head and body responses were markedly lower than for whole monkey images, and the difference between zero versus straight and left versus right angle decoding was absent for sums. In contrast, mSTS showed similar accuracies for sums and whole images, suggesting no genuine encoding of head-body angle in mSTS. This indicates that the head-body angle signal in aSTS requires the simultaneous presence of head and body.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this control analysis without critique. Reviewer 2 notes the study used 'Multiple experiments, control conditions, and detailed analyses' that 'thoroughly examined various factors that could affect the decoding results,' which would include these sum analyses. The logic of this control is not questioned by any reviewer, and it supports the main integration claims.

results.result: The median MSIs (multisensory integration indices) for both poses and regions were smaller than 0, indicating subadditive responses. Surprisingly, some neurons responded to either headless body or head but not to the whole monkey containing the same parts (MSI close to -1). Only a minority of neurons (4.3-6.2%) showed strong superadditive responses (MSI 0.9-1.0).
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question these MSI findings. The subadditive nature of responses is implicitly accepted as part of the broader integration story. Reviewer 2's statement that neurons 'integrate head and body information in a nonlinear way' encompasses both super- and sub-additive interactions. No concerns are raised about the MSI methodology or interpretation.

results.result: Head-body orientation tuning generalized across poses and orientations. The same population of neurons could decode the angle between head and body irrespective of the orientation of the configuration, with marked generalization across orientations observed for P1. This generalization would not be expected if local features of individual images were employed by the classifier.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the generalization findings. Reviewer 1 notes 'using two types of body postures (sitting, standing), they show a correlation in head-body angle between postures, suggesting that monkey orientation might be more meaningful to these neurons than precise posture.' This directly supports the generalization claims. No concerns are raised about the cross-pose or cross-orientation analyses.

results.result: Distance matrices showed evidence for mirror-symmetric responses for lateral head and body orientations. The population of aSTS neurons showed lower sensitivity to mirror-symmetrical views for heads and bodies. Mirror symmetry may have contributed to the lower decoding of head-body angles differing only in sign, though this cannot fully explain the decoding pattern.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the mirror symmetry findings as part of the explanation for the sign-insensitivity. Reviewer 1 explicitly mentions the study's findings about 'invariance to mirror symmetry.' The authors' caveat that mirror symmetry cannot fully explain the pattern is not challenged, suggesting reviewers find the nuanced interpretation appropriate.

results.result: Neuron-dropping analysis for zero versus straight angle decoding in aSTS suggested less than half of neurons contributed positively. The 10 'best' neurons showed diverse tuning profiles, with at least 50% showing significant effects of head-body angle (more than expected by chance at 16%), suggesting population coding of head-body orientation angle.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not critique this analysis. Reviewer 2 notes 'The decoding methods effectively and consistently revealed the encoding of head-body angles in the anterior STS neurons,' which encompasses the neuron-dropping results. The population coding interpretation aligns with reviewers' overall acceptance of the distributed encoding mechanism.

results.result: The highest decoding occurred for zero versus straight angles (frequent versus anatomically impossible configuration). All well-decodable angle differences consisted of possible versus impossible angles. However, no significant effect of head-body angle on mean response strength was observed, and neurons responded equally strongly to anatomically possible and impossible configurations. The anatomical possibility factor may explain better decoding for absolute angle differences, though dissociating this from mirror symmetry is not trivial.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings without critique. The observation that anatomically impossible configurations elicit similar response magnitudes but can be decoded based on population patterns is implicitly accepted as part of the population coding mechanism. No reviewer questions the interpretation regarding anatomical possibility versus response strength.

results.result: Decoding of whole-monkey orientation was present in both mSTS and aSTS, aligning with previous studies. The decoding of head and body orientation was better in mSTS compared to aSTS, consistent with prior work.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm this finding as consistent with the literature. Reviewer 1 notes 'mSTS neurons show more specialization for head or body orientation,' which aligns with the better decoding of individual orientations in mSTS. This result is treated as confirmatory rather than novel.

results.result: Based on the electrophysiological data, one would predict that behavioral discrimination of head-body orientation angle would be more accurate for zero versus straight angles compared to right versus left angles, though this remains to be tested psychophysically.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly notes 'it's unclear how the neural representation relates to the animal's perception. Behavioural experiments using the same set of stimuli could help address this question.' This directly addresses the untested behavioral prediction. While reviewers accept the neural findings, they recognize the behavioral link remains speculative and untested.

results.result: Background claims establishing the research context: face and body processing are often studied separately despite natural integration; previous studies showed face-body interactions in humans and monkeys; head and body orientation are important social cues; behavioral body-inversion effects have been observed; and face-body interactions are proposed to be more prominent in anterior IT, leading to the hypothesis of stronger head-body interactions in aSTS.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the background and motivation without critique. The editor notes the study 'examines the neuronal mechanisms underlying visual perception of integrated face and body cues' using an 'innovative paradigm,' implicitly accepting the rationale. Reviewer 1 states the results 'expand prior work on the role of Anterior STS fundus face area in face-body integration,' confirming the background context.

results.result: Methodological details: recordings were made from fMRI-defined patches in aSTS and mSTS in two monkeys; neurons were selected based on responses to monkeys/faces/bodies versus objects; sample sizes were 98 aSTS and 100 mSTS neurons in experiment 1, and 497 aSTS and 1856 mSTS units in experiment 2; averaged responses were strongest for monkey images, followed by body and face, and weakest for objects.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the methodological approach. Reviewer 2 states 'The use of electrophysiological recordings from fMRI-defined areas elucidated the mechanism of head-body angle encoding at the level of local neuronal populations.' Reviewer 3 notes 'Combining fMRI and electrophysiology, they recorded responses of visual neurons.' The experimental design is praised as 'thoughtfully constructed and detailed' (Reviewer 2).

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate the core finding of nonlinear head-body integration in STS neurons (C2, C34, C35, C36, C7). OpenEval provides detailed statistical validation (two-way ANOVAs, p-values, correlation analyses), while peer reviewers affirm the finding without methodological concerns. Both mark as SUPPORTED with high agreement.

Both address regional differences between aSTS and mSTS (C3, C50, C112). OpenEval focuses on decoding patterns across experiments (C49-C51, C72-C74), while peer review emphasizes position tolerance and transformation from mSTS to aSTS (C37-C46). Overlapping claims C3, C50, C112 show agreement on regional specialization. Both SUPPORTED.

OpenEval R2 addresses decoding of head-body angles (C49-C51, C72-C74), while peer R3 addresses the same decoding findings plus mirror symmetry limitations (C4, C5, C49, C51, C52, C58, C63-C65, C72-C74, C76, C101-C102). Substantial overlap on decoding accuracy and robustness across experiments. Both SUPPORTED.

OpenEval R7 evaluates correlation analyses and reliability controls for regional differences (C37-C41), which peer R2 incorporates as part of broader regional specialization findings (C37-C46). Both affirm position tolerance is greater in aSTS with appropriate statistical controls. Both SUPPORTED.

Both evaluate sum control analyses (C78-C83). OpenEval details how summed responses in aSTS produced lower accuracy and no angle discrimination, ruling out simple summation. Peer review accepts these controls as part of thorough examination of factors affecting decoding. Both SUPPORTED with strong agreement.

Both evaluate body inversion effects (C6, C85, C88-C93, C98, C120, C122, C125). OpenEval provides detailed statistical evidence (Wilcoxon tests, p-values, accuracy drops), while peer review affirms this as one of three main findings and notes it as novel at single-unit level. Both SUPPORTED.

OpenEval R5 addresses mirror symmetry and sign-insensitivity (C63-C65, C101-C105), while peer R3 addresses broader decoding patterns including mirror symmetry challenges (C4, C5, C49, C51, C52, C58, C63-C65, C72-C74, C76, C101-C102). Overlap on C63-C65, C101-C102 shows agreement that mirror-symmetric configurations are difficult to differentiate. Both SUPPORTED.

OpenEval R5 includes mirror symmetry findings (C63-C65, C101-C105), while peer R8 specifically addresses mirror symmetry as partial explanation (C66-C70, C103-C105). Overlap on C103-C105 shows agreement that mirror symmetry contributes but cannot fully explain sign-insensitivity. Both SUPPORTED.

Both evaluate distance matrix analyses showing mirror symmetry (C67-C68). OpenEval notes neural mirror symmetry matches stimulus symmetry, peer review accepts this as part of explanation for sign-insensitivity. Both SUPPORTED with agreement on the finding.

Perfect overlap on MSI findings (C29-C33). OpenEval details median MSI < 0, distribution of values, and surprising finding about natural configurations with negative MSI. Peer review accepts subadditive responses as part of nonlinear integration without critique. Both SUPPORTED.

OpenEval R16 addresses generalization across poses (C47-C48), while peer R7 addresses broader generalization findings (C48, C53, C61, C95, C100). Overlap on C48 shows agreement on cross-pose generalization. Both SUPPORTED.

OpenEval R22 addresses orientation-invariant decoding (C100), while peer R7 addresses multiple generalization findings including C100. Both affirm that head-body angle encoding generalizes across viewpoints. Both SUPPORTED.

OpenEval R13 addresses inference about configural encoding (C94-C95), while peer R7 addresses generalization findings including C95. Both support the interpretation that configural rather than local features drive decoding. Both SUPPORTED.

OpenEval R8 addresses differential performance and centering generalization (C58-C61), while peer R7 addresses broader generalization including C61. Overlap on C61 shows agreement on the role of centering generalization. Both SUPPORTED.

Perfect overlap on neuron-dropping analyses (C54-C57). OpenEval details quantitative characterization of best neurons and population coding interpretation. Peer review accepts this as part of effective decoding methods. Both SUPPORTED.

Both evaluate findings about anatomically possible vs. impossible configurations (C106-C109). OpenEval notes the pattern and acknowledges limitations in dissociating factors. Peer review accepts findings about anatomical possibility and response patterns. OpenEval also includes C114, C117-C118 on mean response effects. Both SUPPORTED.

OpenEval R25 addresses mean response effects and population-level discriminability (C114, C117-C118), while peer R10 addresses anatomical possibility findings (C106-C109, C114, C117-C118, C127). Overlap on C114, C117-C118 shows agreement that information is in population patterns, not mean responses. Both SUPPORTED.

OpenEval R31 addresses speculation about experience and inversion effects (C127-C128), marked as UNCERTAIN. Peer R10 includes C127 as part of accepted findings about anatomical possibility. OpenEval appropriately labels C127-C128 as speculative, while peer review does not separately critique this speculation.

Perfect overlap on replication of individual orientation decoding (C110-C111). OpenEval notes consistency with literature, peer review affirms as confirmatory finding about mSTS specialization. Both SUPPORTED.

Perfect overlap on behavioral prediction (C119). Both mark as UNCERTAIN/untested. OpenEval notes it requires future behavioral testing, peer reviewer explicitly states behavioral experiments are needed to address the perception question. Strong agreement on uncertainty.

OpenEval R19 reports sample sizes for experiment 2 (C71), while peer R14 addresses broader methodological approach including C71. Both accept the sample size documentation as straightforward. Both SUPPORTED.

OpenEval R20 addresses experiment 2 replication of regional differences (C75-C77), while peer R3 addresses decoding findings including C76. Overlap on C76 shows agreement on regional differences in experiment 2. Both SUPPORTED.

OpenEval R21 addresses reliability control for sum analyses (C80), while peer R5 addresses broader sum control analyses including C80. Both accept that reliability data rules out alternative explanations. Both SUPPORTED.

OpenEval R11 provides specific quantitative accuracy values for inversion effects (C89), while peer R4 addresses broader inversion findings including C89. Both support robust body-inversion effects. Both SUPPORTED.

OpenEval R30 summarizes inversion effect patterns (C125), while peer R4 addresses broader inversion findings including C125. Both support the pattern of inversion effects across stimulus types. Both SUPPORTED.

OpenEval R29 addresses methodological improvement with unbiased selection (C121-C122), while peer R4 addresses inversion findings including C122. Both note the unbiased selection strengthens interpretation. Both SUPPORTED.

OpenEval R27 relates findings to literature on temporal cortex organization (C113), while peer R2 addresses regional differences including C113. Both place results in broader context of STS organization. Both SUPPORTED.

OpenEval R10 evaluates subdivision analyses by selectivity (C84) showing decoding is not driven by specific subpopulations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though this supports the broader integration claims accepted by reviewers.

OpenEval R12 evaluates isolated body parts analyses (C86-C87) showing inversion effects are more consistent for whole bodies. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though this is part of the inversion findings accepted in peer R4.

OpenEval R17 evaluates control analysis ruling out response magnitude explanation (C62). No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though peer reviewers accept the thorough control analyses generally.
OpenEval R26 contextualizes differences from previous work (C115-C116) regarding recording location and experimental manipulation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

Peer R13 evaluates background, motivation, and rationale (C1, C8-C22, C24-C25) as SUPPORTED. No corresponding OpenEval result found - OpenEval focused on empirical claims rather than background/motivation claims.
